questions.q: What is the primary difference between the lending window of the IMF and that of the World Bank in terms of time horizon and purpose?
questions.a: Correct answer: The IMF provides short-to-medium-term financing (typically 1–5 years) to address balance-of-payments crises and stabilise macroeconomic conditions, while the World Bank provides long-term loans (15–30 years) for specific development projects (infrastructure, education, health) and structural reforms. A wrong answer that swaps the time horizons or purposes reveals confusion between crisis firefighting (IMF) and developmental lending (World Bank) — a fundamental distinction tested in both board and CUET questions.

questions.q: Why does the IMF's quota-based voting system lead to accusations of "democratic deficit"? Explain with reference to the distribution of voting power.
questions.a: Correct answer: Quotas are based on a country's economic size (GDP, openness, reserves, variability), so wealthy countries hold a majority of votes. The G7 alone controls ~45% of IMF votes; the US has de facto veto (16.5% > 15% threshold for major decisions). Developing countries, despite representing most of the world's population, hold a minority share. A wrong answer that claims "one country one vote" or ignores the 15% veto threshold shows misunderstanding of the weighted voting mechanism that underpins North-South governance critiques.

questions.q: A country experiencing a sudden capital flight and currency collapse approaches the IMF. The IMF approves a Stand-By Arrangement with conditions: reduce fiscal deficit from 8% to 3% of GDP in two years, float the exchange rate, and remove fuel subsidies. Identify the specific IMF lending instrument and explain the rationale behind each condition.
questions.a: Correct answer: Instrument = Stand-By Arrangement (SBA), the IMF's workhorse crisis-lending tool. Rationale: (1) Fiscal consolidation restores investor confidence and reduces need for monetary financing; (2) Floating the exchange rate stops reserve bleed and corrects misalignment; (3) Removing fuel subsidies targets inefficient spending that benefits the rich disproportionately. A wrong answer that names "Structural Adjustment Facility" (concessional, for low-income countries) or omits the macroeconomic logic behind each condition shows inability to apply IMF conditionality framework to real cases.

questions.q: Compare the governance structure of the IMF and World Bank. Why has the "gentlemen's agreement" on leadership (European IMF MD, American World Bank President) survived despite demands for merit-based selection?
questions.a: Correct answer: Both have a Board of Governors (ministerial level), Executive Board (24 Directors), and professional staff led by Managing Director (IMF) / President (World Bank). The informal agreement persists because: (1) US holds veto power in both; (2) Europe collectively holds enough votes to block alternatives; (3) emerging economies (China, India, Brazil) are divided on a single candidate; (4) major shareholders fear losing influence if selection becomes truly open. A wrong answer that describes formal election procedures without addressing the political economy of the informal bargain misses the core governance critique.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "IMF conditionality during the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis deepened the recession and violated national sovereignty." Use evidence from at least two affected countries.
questions.a: Correct evaluation: Partially valid. In Thailand and Indonesia, IMF insisted on premature fiscal tightening (surplus targets) and high interest rates while corporate sectors were collapsing, turning a currency crisis into a deep recession. Closure of insolvent banks without deposit insurance triggered panic. However, Korea's faster recovery followed adoption of IMF-recommended financial restructuring. The sovereignty critique holds because conditionality intrudes on domestic policy space (tax, spending, labour laws) without democratic accountability. A wrong answer that either fully endorses or fully rejects conditionality without country-specific nuance fails the evaluative requirement.

questions.q: Draft a reform proposal for IMF quota redistribution that would increase developing-country voice while preserving the institution's financial credibility. Specify the formula variables and transition mechanism.
questions.a: Good answer includes: (1) Formula: blend of GDP (PPP 50%, market 30%), trade openness (10%), reserves (5%), population (5%) to weight emerging economies higher; (2) Transition: ad hoc quota increases for dynamic economies (China, India, Brazil) funded by voluntary reductions from over-represented Europeans; (3) Safeguard: maintain 85% supermajority for key decisions so US veto remains; (4) Review every 5 years. Poor answer proposes "one country one vote" (destroys financial backing) or ignores the need for US/Europe buy-in, showing lack of practical reform design.
